clean_check: Full re-read of every changed/new file (.github/workflows/deploy.yml in full, .github/workflows/test.yml in full, docker-compose.prod.yml and docker-compose.yml in full, client/nginx.conf in full) plus cross-referenced callers: server/internal/handler/routes.go, middleware.go (RequireSameOrigin/originAllowed), auth.go, auth_test.go, access_test.go, config.go, and client/src/utils/yandexAuth.js. Hunted: A01 access control (sameOrigin gate on /auth/refresh unchanged, verified via routes.go:88 and access_test.go:948 mutating-path coverage), A02 crypto (no key material touched), A03 injection (migration loop uses static glob filenames, no interpolated user input; DB user-rotation heredoc in deploy.yml unchanged by this diff), A04 insecure design (CI gate design — test job precedes deploy via needs:, reusable workflow correctly scoped), A05 misconfiguration (nginx header hygiene, CORS/permissions blocks), A06 vulnerable components (action versions, mariadb:11.4 tag), A07 auth failures (n/a — no app code changed), A08 integrity (CI/CD pipeline changes, hardcoded CI-only DB creds evaluated for supply-chain/log-exposure risk), A09 logging (root password on command line vs GHA log echoing), A10 SSRF (n/a, no new user-controlled URL fetch). Hardcoded-secret scan run for API_KEY=/SECRET=/PASSWORD=/TOKEN=/base64 blobs/connection strings across the 5 changed files plus the new test.yml — only hit is the intentionally-disclosed CI-internal mariadb credentials, addressed as finding 2. No prod secret, key, or token literal found in any changed file. Two minor observations below; neither blocks this task, both pre-existing/adjacent conditions rather than vulnerabilities this diff introduces.

findings.category: A08:2021 Software and Data Integrity Failures
findings.title: Third-party GitHub Actions pinned to mutable version tags, not commit SHAs
findings.description: deploy.yml and test.yml pin actions/checkout@v4, actions/setup-go@v5, docker/setup-buildx-action@v3, docker/login-action@v3, docker/build-push-action@v5, appleboy/ssh-action@v1.0.3, appleboy/scp-action@v0.1.7 by version tag. Tags are mutable — the publisher (or an attacker who compromises the publisher's account) can repoint a tag to different code without the pin changing. appleboy/ssh-action and appleboy/scp-action are the two steps that receive secrets.SSH_PRIVATE_KEY and drive an authenticated SSH session against the prod host, making them the highest-value targets for this class of supply-chain risk in this repo. This condition pre-dates Task 9 (all these action references were already present in deploy.yml before this task's diff; test.yml is new but follows the same existing convention) and Task 9's actual instructions do not ask for action pinning, so this is reported as a pre-existing/adjacent observation, not a regression introduced by this task.
findings.impact: If an upstream action's tag is repointed to malicious code (compromised maintainer account or registry), the next CI run silently executes it with access to SSH_PRIVATE_KEY, GHCR credentials, and all prod secrets exported via env:/envs:.
findings.recommendation: Pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA (e.g. appleboy/ssh-action@<40-char-sha> # v1.0.3) and use Dependabot/Renovate to keep the SHA pins current. Out of scope for this task; flagging for a future infra hardening pass.

findings.category: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
findings.title: CI-internal MariaDB root password appears in workflow source as a literal, not a masked GitHub secret
findings.description: test.yml hardcodes MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD: ci_root as a plain YAML value (job-level env, service env, and the --health-cmd option string all repeat it in cleartext), and the 'Apply migrations' step runs mariadb -uroot -p"${MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD}" .... Because the value is not registered via GitHub's secrets: context, GitHub Actions' log-masking (which redacts registered secret values wherever they appear in step output) does not apply to it. In the normal case this is harmless: the literal 'ci_root' is already visible to anyone who can read the workflow file, so nothing is 'leaked' by it also appearing in a log. The only incremental exposure is if some future edit adds verbose tracing (set -x) or an error path that echoes the full command line (e.g. a mariadb client error dump) to a job log that gets shared outside the org (e.g. pasted into a public bug report) — at that point the same literal would appear again, which is a non-issue only as long as it stays scoped to this throwaway per-job container and is never reused as a real credential anywhere.
findings.impact: None today (container is ephemeral, per-job, not reachable outside the runner, and never touches prod data — confirmed no naming or value collision with docker-compose.prod.yml's DB_ROOT_PASSWORD/DB_USER/DB_PASSWORD, which are sourced from GitHub secrets under different variable names: DB_* vs MARIADB_*). Would only become a real issue if someone later reuses 'ci_root'/'poshivon'/'poshivon' as an actual credential elsewhere, or if the mariadb service is ever changed to expose 3306 beyond the job's lifetime/network.
findings.recommendation: No action required given current throwaway scope. If this pattern is copy-pasted into a workflow that talks to anything persistent, replace the literal with a GitHub Actions secret so masking applies, or generate a random password per run.

targeted_check_results.1_ci_credentials_vs_prod_secrets: PASS — test.yml uses MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD/MARIADB_DATABASE/MARIADB_USER/MARIADB_PASSWORD (values ci_root/poshivon_test/poshivon/poshivon), a distinct variable namespace from docker-compose.prod.yml's DB_HOST/DB_PORT/DB_NAME/DB_USER/DB_PASSWORD/DB_ROOT_PASSWORD (sourced from GitHub secrets via deploy.yml env:/envs:). No name collision, no value reuse. Comment in test.yml:32-34 explicitly documents the container is CI-internal, job-scoped, and intentionally does not reference prod secrets. Container port 3306 is exposed only on the GitHub-hosted runner's own (non-publicly-routable) network for the job's lifetime.
targeted_check_results.2_envs_allowlist: PASS — diff shows CONTACT_EMAIL inserted mid-list (after DEEPSEEK_MAX_RETRIES, before CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS) in both env: (deploy.yml:109) and envs: (deploy.yml:131). Verified the full envs: string against the full env: block line-by-line: all 27 other names (IMAGE_OWNER through GHCR_TOKEN) are present, unchanged, correctly comma-separated with no stray/missing commas, and every name in envs: has a matching env: entry and vice versa. No unrelated var added or dropped.
targeted_check_results.3_nginx_proxy_swap: PASS — new location = /auth/refresh blocks in both .github/workflows/deploy.yml:189-195 (proxy_pass http://poshivon_app:8080) and client/nginx.conf (proxy_pass http://app:8080) carry the same 4 proxy_set_header lines (Host, X-Real-IP, X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto) as the neighboring /auth/status /auth/me /auth/logout /auth/yandex/code blocks — textually identical shape. location = /auth/yandex removed from both files (grep confirms zero remaining /auth/yandex proxy entries; only /auth/yandex/code, which is a different route for the code-exchange step, and /auth/refresh remain). Backend-side cross-check: server/internal/handler/routes.go:80 explicitly documents no /auth/yandex mux entry exists (Task 4's implicit-OAuth removal), and auth_test.go:869-872 asserts POST /auth/yandex now returns 404 from the backend — the removed nginx proxy entry was correctly dead. RequireSameOrigin (middleware.go:183-234) does NOT rely on X-Forwarded-Proto or r.TLS for its same-origin fallback — Decision 8, documented inline at middleware.go:188-190, explicitly distrusts X-Forwarded-Proto for this exact reason (spoofable by whoever sends Origin too) and instead takes scheme from the COOKIE_SECURE config value. So the presence/absence of X-Forwarded-Proto on the /auth/refresh proxy block has no bearing on RequireSameOrigin's security property either way; the header is forwarded anyway for shape-consistency with neighbors, which is correct practice for any other scheme-sensitive code downstream (e.g. cookie Secure attribute logic, redirect construction) but not a same-origin-check dependency. client/src/utils/yandexAuth.js only calls /auth/refresh and /auth/yandex/code — no remaining client reference to the deleted /auth/yandex path.
targeted_check_results.4_contact_email_fallback_deviation: PASS, not a security concern — CONTACT_EMAIL is the only var in the .env heredoc (deploy.yml:239-266) using the ${VAR:-} fallback form (line 251); every other var (IMAGE_OWNER through GRAFANA_ADMIN_PASSWORD) keeps the plain ${VAR} form, confirming the deviation was scoped to exactly this one var as claimed. Functionally: under GitHub Actions, a secret reference (${{ secrets.X }}) that doesn't exist evaluates to an empty string during expression evaluation, not an omitted assignment — so the env: block always defines CONTACT_EMAIL (possibly empty), and bash's `set -u` does not treat 'defined but empty' as an unbound-variable error. This means the ${CONTACT_EMAIL:-} fallback is not strictly load-bearing against the specific 'secret doesn't exist' failure mode described, but it is also not harmful: worst case it is redundant. No other secret was given this treatment, so no unintended masking of a required credential's absence. CONTACT_EMAIL falling back to empty is confirmed as the documented, legitimate default in server/internal/config/config.go:83 (envOrDefault("CONTACT_EMAIL", "")) — an attacker cannot leverage this to degrade a security-relevant secret, since no other var shares the fallback and CONTACT_EMAIL itself carries no access-control or crypto function (display-only, no-access banner).
targeted_check_results.5_migration_apply_step: Not a named risk in the brief but checked incidentally — the 'Apply migrations' loop (test.yml:68-75) iterates a static glob (server/migrations/*.up.sql) with no user-controlled input; correctly excludes 0001_init.sql (PostgreSQL-only, confirmed present in the migrations directory and correctly not matching the *.up.sql glob). No injection surface.
